function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact numbers right now. But you can quickly find out yourself with one of the following methods: | Method | How to do it | |--------|--------------| | **Web site** | Visit (or ) and click “Go” / “Start.” The page will ping a nearby server and report download/upload speeds and latency. | | **Windows PowerShell** | Open PowerShell and run:
`Test-NetConnection -ComputerName www.google.com -InformationLevel Detailed`
This gives you latency and packet loss, but not throughput. For a full speed test you’ll need a third‑party tool. | | **Command‑line tool (speedtest‑cli)** | If you have Python installed, you can install the Speedtest CLI:
`pip install speedtest-cli`
Then run:
`speedtest`
It will automatically pick a nearby server and report download/upload speeds. | | **Router’s admin page** | Many modern routers expose a “Speed Test” button in their web interface. Log into your router’s admin panel (usually at or ) and look for a diagnostics or status section. | Pick whichever feels easiest. Once you run the test, you’ll see something like: ``` Download: 85.23 Mbit/s Upload: 12.45 Mbit/s Ping: 18 ms ``` Those numbers give you a snapshot of your current broadband performance. If you’re troubleshooting, run the test several times at different times of day to spot patterns.
